title: RoutingBench: Can Evidence-Based Agentic Routing Analysis Scale to Production Networks?
claim: A small local configuration change can reroute traffic globally, so analysis must find the relevant evidence across many devices.
layout: Single wide panel: topology graph center, config snippets left and right
description: A wide network diagram shows rounded boxes for routers, linked by gray physical links. The chain runs from Src through Edge-1, Aggr-1, Core-1, Border-1 and Peer-A to Dst. Branches lead to Peer-B, and to Core-2, Border-2 and FW. Blue arrows mark paths before the change. Red dotted arrows mark paths after the change, which detour from Aggr-1 through Core-2, Border-2 and FW to Dst. A legend box in the middle explains the line styles. At lower left, a purple-bordered config box for Aggr-1.cfg shows a local-preference edit: 50 in red is replaced by 200 in green. At right, two boxes show unchanged config snippets (static route, MED) for Border 2 and the peer and firewall devices, labelled in red as unchanged. The eye goes first to the colored path arrows, then to the config edit.
caption: An example of routing-path analysis. In this example, a local BGP LP change on router Aggr-1 would direct the queried endpoint-prefix pair onto a globally different path. Along the new path, determining the path outcome requires reasoning across network devices and protocols.
abstract: Recent advances in AI models and agentic technologies make AI for network operations (NetOps) within reach. However, scalability remains a key bottleneck of agentic NetOps when analyzing hyperscale production networks, which comprise hundreds of datacenters, each housing thousands of network devices. This challenge is rooted in the requirement of many NetOps tasks that must conduct global reasoning on how a local change of device behavior affects all relevant routing paths, known as routing-path analysis . In this paper, we reframe the scalability bottleneck as discovering the relevant configuration evidence rather than understanding protocols or constructing the entire network topologies. We evaluate how different agentic approaches, namely in-context learning, iterative reasoning, and agent skills, can scale routing-path analysis to large, complex networks. We present RoutingBench for evaluating agentic routing-path analysis based on evidence discovery. It generates fat-tree-based datacenter topologies with six single routing change types and compound changes, using metrics like path analysis correctness, token cost, and runtime to evaluate agents. Our results show that, given the knowledge of topology and routing-policy design of the analyzed networks, agentic path analysis based on configuration evidence discovery achieves an accuracy of 98.8% on fat-tree networks of 50K routers, significantly outreaching the scalability of traditional symbolic analysis. Meanwhile, RoutingBench reveals the boundary of AI agent capability on complex inter-datacenter networks and compound changes, posing open challenges for AI and agentic research.
